questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: English speaking and in Europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of information (more than I needed), it would have been nice to recive one sigle mail.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not really any.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found the room I rented through the app Spareroom. I wrote 30 different people and she was the only one really answering me.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Most students live in some shared apartment or student accomondation. A lot of them just around The Meadows. I lived on the other side og King's Bouildings (the campus where I studied). I would very mush have prefered to live closer to the center - besides my actuel lectures it was here that most things happend with societies and other stuff. It also felt a bit isolating not living with other students. I found private accomondation becouse it, in my understandig, was not certain that I could get something trough the university, but it seemed like everybody got something (including me, but only twp weeks before the semester started, so at that time I had other plans). But my housing was probably cheaper than the student accomondation. It seemed like most of the (non-exchange) students lived in student accomondations the first year but then prefered to find some shared appartments.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When officially approved for the exchange, you applied for each course (and some extra) and send a separate document with priorities. After getting (some) of them it was possible to wish for change. But it was way easier just to change the courses the first two weeks after the semester started!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You get an academic cohost who can help you once arrived :)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Succsessful

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I did not manage to change into the courses I wanted beforehand, but it was easier to change once arrived. I got some of the courses I applied for rejected, instead of trying to convince them that I had the prerequisites. 
In the first two weeks of the semester it is allowed to change your courses (ass long as there are still spots available, which there where in all the courses I wanted). Use these two weeks to hear what other students, who have taken the courses or know someone who has, say about them!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Level. One course a bit harder, but in general the courses easier, but exam harder (compared to the rest of the course).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For most of my courses there were one tutorial exercise with four lectures, so we have more tutorials in Copenhagen. (Some of) The lectures were more interactive in Edinburgh – two of them had the structure of students submitting questions beforehand and then the lecture was just about answering them.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Category Theory: A really nice course! Quite time-consuming and abstract, so you must like this, but the lecturer was really good and motivating. 
Combinatorics and Graph Theory: Cozy enough but not that advanced. 
Commutative Algebra: Some of the curriculum was already covered by Algebra 2 at home, except the coursenotes in Edinburgh was a bit confusing and unstructured (but the lecturer really sweet!). 
Fundamentals of Operational research: Nothing really happened in the lectures, but the topics were not too bad.
Informatics 1 – Introduction to Computation: A first year programming course in Haskell. The tutorial exercises was quite cozy, the rest a bit waste of time (what you can expect of a first year course).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Category theory! (The same lecturer are having Axomatic set theory every second year, and category theory the other). The rest OK, but you don’t miss out on a lot not having them :)

questions.answer: Not really any.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: A lot of the social stuff happened at a pub, so the money spend on pubs added up quicker than I had expected. Food and a lot of other stuff a bit cheaper than at home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Edinburgh university have A LOT of societies and sports clubs. All of them have (in addition to activities related to the actual theme of the club) some different socials (I vent to pub quiz, ceilidh dance (Scottish danse), pub crawl, sock wrestling (don’t ask) etc. ). You can meet all the different clubs and societies in the welcome week.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I was a part of:
Math-society – they had some academic activities and some different socials, it was nice (especially in the first couple of weeks) to have a place to meet some of the other math students that I saw around in the lectures. 
Canue club – we vent river kayaking, which was really cool! It was a lot of the same people, they where really nice, but most of them had known each other for a long time 
Moutainering club – this was a really big society, I felt like it was new people I met every time I showed up for something. Had activities almost every day of the week (and a camping trip every other weekend) (every Tuesday there was hill running and Wednesday wild swimming in the morning and bouldering in the evening, and Thursdays some social). Focused a lot on climbing. People showed often up in groups.
ESN (Erasmus) – A joined their trip to the Isle of Skye. A really beautiful trip!! But I am not sure I would recommend it – it was a lot of time in a bus, and very touristy (having 20 minutes breaks to take a lot of pictures and then returning to the bus).  

Dirty weekenders - every sunday they vent doing some gardening (sometimes planting trees) in the area of Edinburgh. Some very sweet people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join some societies! But I do think I focused a bit to much in the local students instead of exchange students – they have the same mentality as you about only being there for a short time, so it is easier to make a friendgroup from this, than people who already have a friendgroup.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the highlands.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, not that much of a difference except in English. And maybe some more smalltalk with people in general.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a society

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I found the welcome week a bit challenging. A lot of things happened during the week and I met a lot of people I only talked to once, and not really any I ended up becoming friends with. A lot of the social activities was focused around the societies, and not the studies.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: A lot of really friendly people

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Have a look at the welcome week schedule before start so it doesn’t seem as overwhelming

Maybe reach out to someone from your own university before going just so you have someone you know from the beginning

Its okay to feel lonely at times, you are in a completely new country without your network from home. Sometimes I felt there was some pressure about having the best semester of your life, but remember that it is also an everyday life you are going to have.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I have written what I could think of in the previous questions :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To be taken out of the everyday life I know and rethink what I actually like to do and spend my time on, instead of just what I usually do.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: For me it was to get to know some people good enough to feel relaxed around them, I am lucky to have some great friends from home that I missed a bit.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
